question: What is the primary shift in meaning when moving from the term "compliance" to "adherence"?

options.A: Moving from herbal remedies to orthodox pharmaceutical treatments
options.B: Transitioning from hospital administration to home care delivery
options.C: Changing the frequency of daily medication administration times
options.D: Shifting from passive patient obedience to active partnership

explanation: Adherence emphasizes that the patient actively participates in and agrees with the treatment plan, unlike the older concept of compliance which implies passive obedience. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h1)

question: What threshold of medication intake is typically used to separate optimal adherence from suboptimal adherence?

options.A: Taking less than 80 percent of prescribed doses
options.B: Skipping every weekend dose of a maintenance drug
options.C: Failing to refill prescriptions within 24 hours
options.D: Missing more than two consecutive days of therapy

explanation: Clinical research and practice generally define suboptimal adherence as taking less than 80 percent of the total prescribed medication regimen over a given period. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h1)

question: What major public health threat is directly worsened by irregular or incomplete antibiotic use?

options.D: Rapid depletion of national drug stockpiles

explanation: Incomplete courses of antimicrobials allow hardier microorganisms to survive, replicate, and develop resistance against standard pharmacological agents. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h2)

question: A patient with chronic hypertension stops taking their antihypertensive drugs intermittently because they feel fine. What is the most likely physiological consequence?

options.A: Fluctuating blood pressure readings and eventual target organ damage
options.B: Immediate development of systemic drug hypersensitivity syndrome
options.C: Spontaneous regeneration of damaged renal and cardiac tissues
options.D: Permanent stabilization of baseline vascular tone without medication

explanation: Stopping and starting blood pressure medication causes dangerous cardiovascular fluctuations that silently strain blood vessels, the heart, and kidneys over time. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h2)

question: Why do asymptomatic conditions like hypertension present a major challenge to medication adherence?

options.A: Insurance policies refuse to cover drugs for symptomless disorders
options.B: Pharmacists frequently mislabel bottles for silent chronic conditions
options.C: Patients do not feel sick, so they question the necessity of daily pills
options.D: Blood pressure medications only work when physical symptoms appear

explanation: Because silent killers produce no immediate discomfort, patients often fail to see the immediate value of taking bitter or expensive drugs every day. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which barrier is being addressed when a nurse simplifies a patient's regimen from four daily doses to a single once-daily extended-release tablet?
explanation: Reducing the number of daily administrations directly tackles the complexity barrier, making it easier for the client to remember and manage their therapy. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h3)

question: A Nigerian patient with diabetes admits to simultaneously taking local herbal concoctions alongside prescribed hypoglycemic agents. What is the most appropriate initial nursing response?

options.A: Demand that the patient immediately sign a discharge against medical advice form
options.B: Acknowledge the practice non-judgmentally and evaluate for potential herb-drug interactions
options.C: Confiscate all herbal preparations during the clinic visit without explanation
options.D: Scold the patient severely for risking their life with unapproved traditional mixtures

explanation: A non-judgmental approach builds trust, ensuring the patient shares vital information so the nurse can screen for dangerous drug-herb interactions. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is a primary economic driver of poor medication compliance in many Nigerian households?

options.A: Mandatory universal health insurance covering all prescription needs
options.B: Excessive government subsidies causing artificial drug shortages
options.C: Heavy reliance on out-of-pocket payments for healthcare services
options.D: Free pharmaceutical distribution centers overwhelming local markets

explanation: Without comprehensive universal health coverage, out-of-pocket spending forces families to choose between basic survival needs and buying routine medicines. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h4)

question: Which of the following is an example of a direct method for measuring medication adherence?

options.A: Counting the remaining tablets inside the pill container
options.B: Reviewing pharmacy refill dates in the electronic database
options.C: Measuring drug metabolite levels in blood or urine
options.D: Asking the patient how many pills they missed last week

explanation: Direct methods involve biological confirmation that the substance entered the patient's body, such as blood, urine, or directly observed ingestion. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why might relying solely on patient self-reports during clinic visits lead to inaccurate adherence data?

options.A: Recall bias is completely eliminated when patients talk to nurses
options.B: Self-reporting methods automatically measure drug metabolites in the bloodstream
options.C: Pharmacy refill records contradict self-reports by showing zero purchases
options.D: Patients often overestimate their adherence to please the healthcare provider

explanation: Social desirability bias causes many individuals to report perfect adherence because they want to avoid disappointing their doctor or nurse. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of using the "teach-back" method during patient education?

options.A: To force the patient to memorize the generic names of all drugs
options.B: To test the patient's reading speed and formal educational level
options.C: To verify that the patient truly understood the care instructions provided
options.D: To evaluate the nurse's public speaking and presentation skills

explanation: Teach-back requires the patient to explain instructions back in their own words, confirming comprehension rather than just getting a nod of agreement. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h6)

question: Which nursing action best demonstrates culturally sensitive and accessible patient education?

options.A: Reading technical package insert leaflets aloud word-for-word at high speed
options.B: Handing out advanced scientific pharmacology textbooks for independent study
options.C: Using simple language, relatable analogies, and visual aids tailored to the client
options.D: Directing the client to search online medical forums for dosage guidance

explanation: Tailoring communication by avoiding medical jargon and incorporating visual tools ensures that health literacy barriers are actively overcome. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h6)

question: Which physical tool is commonly recommended by nurses to help patients organize multiple daily medications?

options.A: A standard kitchen measuring spoon set
options.C: A weekly pill box or blister pack container

explanation: Weekly pill organizers compartmentalize doses by day and time, making it instantly obvious whether a dose has been taken or missed. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h7)

question: A patient forgets their afternoon medication dose daily because they are busy at work. What is the most practical nursing intervention?

options.A: Instruct the patient to double their morning dose to make up for the afternoon
options.B: Advise the patient to stop working so they can focus on healthcare
options.C: Switch the patient immediately to an intravenous therapy at home
options.D: Help the patient set a digital alarm on their mobile phone for work hours

explanation: A mobile alarm provides an environmental cue right when the patient is busy at work, prompting them to take their scheduled dose on time. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h7)
